parts.title: Sorting scientific papers into subjects: a test of deep learning against two ways of using citations
parts.abstract:
When governments, universities and countries judge how much research is being done, they rely on systems that sort research work and published papers into subjects. Several of these sorting systems are already in use. They need constant updating, because new sorting methods appear and new research topics arise.

One kind of computer method, called a convolutional neural network, belongs to a larger family known as "deep learning". In recent years, these methods have offered new and very effective ways to sort huge collections of text. In this article, we test one deep learning method on more than 40 million scientific articles and on tens of thousands of research journals.

We compare it with two methods that work from citations, the references that papers make to each other. The first, bibliographic coupling, looks at which earlier papers two papers share. The second, direct citation, looks at which papers cite which. We also compare it with sorting done by hand by experts. These citation-based and hand-sorted systems are the established and most widely used approaches in bibliometrics, the study of how research papers are cited and counted. They are also used in many science and innovation policies, such as running competitions for research grants.

Our results show that this first version of a deep learning method performs as well as the citation-based methods, which work by following links between papers. All the methods we present are also on a par with sorting by hand. Somewhat surprisingly, none of the machine learning methods clearly beat direct citation, which is a simple method that passes labels along the citation links.

In conclusion, deep learning is promising. It performed just as well as the other approaches, but it has more room to be improved. For example, a deep neural network that also takes in information from the network of citations is likely to hold the key to an even better way of sorting papers.
parts.introduction_first:
The ways we sort research work and published papers into subjects, and the ways we measure those subjects, quietly but widely shape research policy and every kind of performance check [1, 2]. In these checks, putting a research group's or a university's work into one field of research instead of another can completely change the result. The sorting system, and the choices made in designing it, also decide which other groups are used for comparison and what levels are used as reference points. These reference points are needed to adjust the numbers so that different fields can be compared fairly.

Put simply, nearly every researcher and scholar whose work is judged with these citation-based measures, and even those who only care a little about how often their writing is cited, are affected by design choices in some of the main sorting systems of science that are commonly used to judge research. This is why building sorting systems that are useful and precise matters so much.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

People have argued again and again about the best ways to build and improve the systems that sort science into subjects. These systems are used to organize science on a large scale, including planning science policy, judging research on a large scale and managing research grants. Researchers who study citations tend to prefer systems built from the bottom up, where similar papers are grouped together first and the groups are then joined into larger categories. Science policy bodies and funders, however, still use and create systems built by hand, which depend on the judgment of experts, rather than systems built by computer methods. They do this because the hand-built systems keep things consistent with the long-standing practices of institutions.

In this article, we presented a new way to sort science. It combines deep learning with bibliographic coupling, which links papers that share the same references. This lets it connect two things: sorting each research paper on its own, from the bottom up, and the ready-made categories that already exist.

We gave the three approaches the task of creating a sorting of individual papers from a sorting of journals. On this task, all three performed about as well as experts sorting by hand.

We also think the deep learning approach has great potential to be improved and refined in the future. There are several ways this could happen. One is to try graph neural networks, a type of deep learning that works with networks of links, so that the method can use the network of citations and the network of authors who work together. Another is to build the Herfindahl index, a score of how tightly a paper's references are concentrated in a few subjects, into the loss function, the score the network tries to make as small as it learns. A third is simply to combine bibliographic coupling and direct citation better with the modified character-based neural network we present here.
parts.introduction_rest:
Sorting documents into subjects is as old as libraries themselves. In the great Library of Alexandria, for example, a librarian called Callimachus sorted the works in tables called the "Pinakes". These tables listed subjects such as rhetoric, law, epic, tragedy, comedy, lyric poetry, history, medicine, mathematics, natural science, and a catch-all for everything else [3]. People rarely agree on how to sort things. A new sorting system is usually criticized soon after it is created. This may have started as early as the sharp, aggressive criticism that the Greek playwright Aristophanes wrote about Callimachus's Pinakes [4].

The aim of a sorting system is to put similar documents together in one group, or class. Documents can be alike in many ways, such as the language they are written in or the field they belong to. These many sides of knowledge appear in every description of research. Because of this, sorting systems are needed at different scales, for example for a whole journal or for a single article. There are also different kinds of classes that can be used at the same time to describe research work and published papers, for instance to match how universities or companies are organized. In universities, for example, subjects and faculties sort themselves by the topics they study. So does the All Science Journal Classification of Scopus, a large database of research papers. In contrast, the Medical Subject Headings of the US National Library of Medicine, a thesaurus (a dictionary of subject labels), aims to reflect a mixed bag of subjects and experimental methods.

Every sorting system of intellectual work has trouble with its boundaries, to a greater or lesser degree. In other words, it is hard to say clearly what counts as belonging to a class and what does not. Sorting research documents such as journals and articles does not escape this problem. New knowledge is created all the time, and newer knowledge does not always fit neatly into classes that already exist [5]. These typical difficulties of sorting appear at every scale, although some researchers argue that they are especially troublesome at the level of journals [6, 7]. The problem is "fractal": it repeats itself at every size. A scientific journal could often be placed in more than one class, and the same is true of a scientific article. This leads to arguments about two choices. One is to use sorting schemes in which each item can belong to only one class, which makes reporting easier and clearer. The other is to let each item belong to several classes, which is more true to the real nature of the work.

One reason to use sorting systems in the study of science and in judging research is to capture, understand and discuss how research practices change. Summing things up at a higher level, in a more general form, helps bring out the broad trends and patterns that institutions, government agencies and all kinds of commentators most often study. In bibliometrics, one of the main reasons to sort scientific work and writing is to make citation-based measures comparable. This is needed because different fields have their own habits for who counts as an author and how papers are cited, and because citation patterns change over time [8].

A key feature of a sorting system, especially one used to judge research, is how finely it divides things up. It might sort at the level of journals or articles, or at the level of conferences or presentations. Sorting scientific work at the level of journals and articles has been studied a great deal [9–12]. Sorting at the level of journals often repeats the long-standing habits and names of each field. This makes it easier for some people to use, including research managers, policymakers and funders. It is certainly useful for journal publishers, who need to sort their journals and show them on their websites in a compact way. It can also be used to describe the field in which authors work [13].

There are many cases where sorting journals is useful, but there are also many cases where sorting articles is better and more precise. For example, in bibliometrics it is often useful to sort each article separately in journals that cover many fields, such as PLOS ONE, Nature or Science. Also, some articles published in a journal about cancer, for instance, may be more about surgery than about cancer itself. As a result, sorting at the level of journals is not very precise compared with sorting at the level of articles [6, 8, 10, 11]. Sorting journals is still needed for many uses. Even so, there are several reasons to prefer sorting articles over sorting journals in many situations where research is judged.

Knowledge is changing extremely fast, and this causes real problems for sorting at both the level of journals and the level of articles. For example, the 1findr database [14] lists the content of close to 100,000 research journals that are checked by experts before publication, including journals that are now active and journals that have closed. The Scopus database [15] takes a narrower view of a similar collection. It picks out journals that are highly respected by other researchers, or that are cited most often in their fields, or both (Fig 1). In both databases, the number of articles doubles about every 17 years. This means each database holds as many articles from the last 17 years as from all the years before that.

This fast growth of scientific writing puts a huge strain on the need to sort it. One reason is simply the enormous number of articles that must be sorted every day. Another is that scientific knowledge keeps changing, so new classes have to be added to sorting systems. Sometimes this means rebuilding the whole system and resorting thousands of journals and millions of articles. Doing this work by hand costs far too much money and takes far too long. Precise computer methods for sorting are therefore badly needed.

Librarians have sorted articles by hand for decades, if not centuries. Computer sorting, however, is fairly new, because it needs powerful computers and the ability to collect and describe scientific papers on a large scale [6]. Research carried out since the 1970s has produced a toolkit of sorting approaches. Each is backed by a different amount of evidence, and researchers have to choose a method that suits the things they are sorting. Most computer methods for sorting articles are based on clustering, which means grouping similar items together. They work from the bottom up, and they need quite a lot of extra work afterwards to connect the groups they find to categories that people can understand. Working out the best way to join groups into larger categories is still being developed [11, 12, 16, 17]. Computer sorting methods have also improved thanks to progress in network analysis, which studies networks of links, and in text mining, which means pulling information out of large amounts of text [18–21].

Many methods have been developed and are routinely used in computer science, in the field of natural language processing (which teaches computers to understand human language) and, more recently, in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI). These methods could be very useful in bibliometrics. In particular, deep learning has recently been found to be extremely good at finding patterns in messy, noisy data, as long as the network is trained on enough examples. Yet, despite all the work done so far on computer sorting methods, people who study citations have not yet made lasting use of AI, and especially of deep learning, when they sort papers or group them.

The BioASQ challenge is a notable recent example of deep learning being used in a task related to bibliometrics [22]. However, the researchers and the people who study citations have so far explored this topic side by side, separately. Since 2012, the BioASQ challenge has aimed to encourage methods and systems for sorting biomedical writing into subjects on a large scale. It does this by running a competition in which teams try to automatically give each scientific paper the subject labels from PubMed's MeSH terms, a standard set of medical subject labels [23].

Perhaps surprisingly, none of the 9182 articles published in journals whose names contain "scientomet*", "informetri*" or "bibliometri*" ever mentioned BioASQ in their title, abstract or keywords. Only one of those 9182 papers cites a paper related to BioASQ. We found this with a search in Scopus: "SRCTITLE (scientomet* OR informetri* OR bibliometri*) AND REF (bioasq)". That one paper is not about sorting text.

As we just mentioned, most solutions to the BioASQ challenge now use methods based on deep neural networks. Several of them were based on BERT and BioBERT, two well-known deep learning models [22]. In this paper, we chose to explore a different type of deep neural network, namely a character-based neural network, which reads text one letter at a time. We did this because we felt our task was different from the BioASQ task and less suited to those designs. For example, the level of detail is very different: we are sorting 174 subfields, instead of about 27,000 MeSH terms. Also, the examples we used to train our network are extremely noisy, with an accuracy of 56%.

This noise may seem like a poor design for an experiment, but it is a real part of the task that people who study citations face. Any system or strategy for resorting papers, whether it is meant to sort articles or journals, will need to cope with a noisy training set, because collecting a training set of articles would cost far too much. The last difference is that we used a much larger set of input data, and some of it is harder to break into small pieces, called tokens. For example, it seemed like a poor choice to define tokens for authors' affiliations, for the names of sources cited, or for other very rare and specific words. Even so, these were useful ideas that helped us choose a design for our model. Because they have not been tested, other designs should be explored in future work.

In general, a sorting system is only as good as the ways it is measured and checked [6, 7]. To see how precise a deep learning sorting method could be, we compared its results with two other methods that are often used to map science: bibliographic coupling and direct citation. We judged the comparison with two scores. The first was a score of how tightly a paper's references are concentrated in a few subjects [6]. The second was how well the results agreed with a reference set of papers that had been sorted by hand.

Besides being a new experiment with deep learning, our computer experiment was carried out on a very large scale. Because of limits on computing power, bibliographic coupling has usually been calculated on samples of records rather than on the whole collection in databases such as Scopus and the Web of Science. In this paper, we use deep learning together with bibliographic coupling, mostly on the whole collection of papers in the Scopus database. One advantage of our approach is that it can sort articles, and journals can then be sorted by combining the results. Having a single sorting system that works at both levels lets us compare the sorting of articles directly with the sorting of journals, which earlier studies have rarely done [10]. Finally, and most importantly, most research on sorting systems focuses on creating new ones. This paper instead asks whether computer sorting methods, including AI, can be used to keep existing sorting systems up to date better than sorting by hand.
parts.methods:
## Methods

### Where our data came from

We used a version of the Scopus database, a large online catalogue of scientific papers, that has been specially prepared for counting and sorting research. It was made by Science-Metrix, a company that builds systems for sorting science into subjects. From it we collected the basic details of each scientific article, such as its title and authors, together with its citation data, meaning which papers it cites and which papers cite it. We used the version of the database as it stood on 8 May 2019.

We included papers from three kinds of sources: book series, conference proceedings (the collections of papers presented at scientific meetings) and journals. For book series and journals, we kept only four types of document: articles, conference papers, reviews and short surveys. For conference proceedings, we kept only those labelled as articles, reviews and conference papers. We also removed sources that did not have a valid ISSN, the official number given to journals and other periodicals. Altogether, our experiment used 41 million Scopus publication records.

### The training set

To test our three computer methods for sorting, we needed a ready-made set of categories to sort papers into. We used the journal sorting system made by Science-Metrix as the starting point for the categories that articles and journals would be placed in. This system is available in more than 25 languages. It contains a core set of 15,000 journals and is free to use (see science-metrix.com/classification and the Supporting information). Science-Metrix also uses, internally, a further set of about 15,000 journals. Each of these had fewer than 30 articles when the original sorting system was designed.

In the system, each journal is placed in exactly one of 176 scientific subfields, which are fairly narrow subjects. These subfields are grouped into 22 fields, and the fields are grouped in turn into six domains, which are the broadest areas.

The first version of this sorting system was built from the top down. Its designers looked at the systems used by several major bodies and took the best ideas from them: the US National Science Foundation, the Web of Science (now run by Clarivate, which was Thomson Reuters at the time), the Australian Research Council, the European Science Foundation and the OECD. Journals were first placed in categories based on these systems. They were then run through several rounds of automatic suggestions. These suggestions drew on three kinds of clues: direct citation, Latent Dirichlet Allocation [24] (a statistical method that finds hidden topics in a large collection of texts) and the names of university departments. After each round, people corrected the suggestions by hand [9].

Since then, the original version has not been updated in the last 10 years, apart from new journals being added by hand in the version used for everyday work. As a result, some journals may have drifted away from the subfields they were first placed in. Also, many journals would no doubt be sorted more precisely if the sorting were done again, because the clues would be better. Ten more years of publications mean far more references and citations to work with.

A newer version of this sorting system is now being developed. It is more detailed, with 330 subfields, 33 fields and seven domains. It is not yet used for everyday sorting, but it can be seen in the 1findr database, which lists and describes research papers (see 1findr.com). The methods we tested here were used to build this expanded version. It already gives a category to more than 56,000 journals, and about the same number still need to be sorted. More than 130 million scholarly articles are also waiting to be sorted.

### Sorting individual papers and journals

Many papers on sorting use clustering, a method that builds categories from the bottom up by grouping similar papers together. Our experiment works differently. We took the clues produced by three ways of linking papers and matched them to the existing Science-Metrix categories. We linked papers at the level of individual articles. To decide which category a journal belonged to, we added up all the articles in that journal and gave the journal the subfield that appeared most often.

### Comparing deep learning with two ways of using citations

We wanted to compare the results of our more experimental deep learning method (DL) with two methods that are commonly used in bibliometrics: bibliographic coupling (BC) and direct citation (DC). So we also sorted the articles and journals into the Science-Metrix categories using these two methods.

We compared DL with the other methods in two ways. First, we used concentration scores, which measure how tightly a paper's references are bunched into a few subjects. We worked these out for review articles, both for each article and for each journal. Second, we compared DL with the categories that bibliometrics experts gave to articles by hand.

### Deep learning: a modified character-based convolutional deep neural network

Our sorting method was a convolutional deep neural network that works at the level of characters, meaning the single letters that make up each article's text. Starting from single letters, the model learned words and picked out useful patterns. This character-based approach was developed recently by borrowing ideas from computer vision, the field that lets computers understand pictures, and applying them to sorting text. It has been used on large collections of text, such as the categories built from Wikipedia and the comment logs of Yahoo! Answers [25]. It has been found to be extremely good at finding patterns in noisy data, that is, data full of errors and irregularities.

The model worked best when it was given the following pieces of information: the authors' affiliations (the institutions they work at), the names of the journals in the reference list, the titles of the references, the abstract, the keywords, the title of the paper, and the categories of the papers in the reference list. We cut every piece of information, except the categories of the references, to a fixed maximum length (Table 1). We did not pad them with extra filler text. We then joined all the pieces into one long string of text. This string was itself cut to a maximum length of 3,000 characters. We chose this length because, when we lined up the joined strings from shortest to longest, 98% of them were shorter than it.

Table 1

The information fed into the character-based convolutional deep neural network.

| Branch | Feature | Length

| Text branch | |

| | Title | 175

| | Keywords | 150

| | Authors' affiliations | 450

| | Abstract | 1750

| | Journal title of references | 1000

| | Article title of references | 500

| Subfield branch | |

| | Vector of classifications of a publication's references | 176

The order of the items in this table is the order they appear in the model. The lengths are the longest each piece of information is allowed to be.

Each character was turned into a list of 68 numbers, called a one-hot encoding. In this kind of list, every number is zero except the one at the position that stands for that character, which is set to one. Table 2 shows an example for the word "cab".

Table 2

An example of turning characters into numbers.

| | c | a | b

| a | 0 | 1 | 0

| b | 0 | 0 | 1

| c | 1 | 0 | 0

When we turned characters into numbers, each of the 26 letters of the English alphabet, the 10 Arabic numbers, several punctuation marks (for example "-,;.!?:’_/\|@#$%ˆ&*˜+ = <>()[]{}\), and the space each took up one position in the list. Any character not on this list was turned into a hash sign (#). The subfield was the only piece of information we did not feed into the model as plain text. Instead, we turned it into a list showing what share of each subfield was mentioned in the reference list.

Fig 2 shows how the deep neural network was built. A neural network is made of layers of simple calculating units, called nodes. Between each layer, a rule called an activation function decides how strongly each node passes its signal on. We used a rule called a rectified linear unit, which keeps positive values and turns negative values into zero. After the last layer we used a different rule, called a softmax, which turns the network's output into a set of numbers that add up to one, so they can be read as chances of each category.

The network also used small filters, called kernels, that slide across the text to spot patterns. The kernels were seven characters wide for the first two rounds of filtering and three characters wide for the others. To train the network, we used a method called stochastic gradient descent. It works a bit like walking downhill in the dark: the network takes small steps in whatever direction seems to lower its error, and it adjusts those steps as it goes. The error it tried to make as small as possible was a score called categorical cross-entropy, which measures how far the network's guesses are from the right answers.

We set the size of each step, called the learning rate, to 0.01. We used a nesterov momentum of 0.9, which helps the network keep moving steadily in a good direction instead of wobbling back and forth. We used a decay of 0.000001, which slowly shrinks the momentum over time. The network learned from 64 publications at a time. We counted one full pass through the data, called an epoch, as finished after about 11,000 articles. The network was trained on a random sample of 24,000,000 articles.

Fig 2

How the deep neural network was built.

### Other machine learning methods

Besides deep learning, we also tried three other machine learning methods, so that we could compare them with the established ways of sorting papers using citations. We describe them below, but in the end all three did worse than our deep learning method (the modified character-based convolutional deep neural network). To keep the paper focused on comparing deep learning with the citation-based methods, we do not present the results for these three methods after this section. Readers who are interested can find them in the supplementary material (S1 and S2 Figs, S1 and S3 Tables).

One of the methods we tested was a character-based neural network without the changes described above. Its design followed the small convolutional neural networks developed by Zhang and colleagues (preprint) (20), but here is a short description. The input was a grid of 70 characters, each turned into numbers. This grid went into two layers in a row, each with 256 kernels seven characters wide. Each of these two layers was followed by a maxpooling layer, which keeps only the strongest signal in each small window, with a window width of 3, and then by a rectified linear unit. After these first two layers came four more layers, each with 256 features but this time three characters wide and without maxpooling.

Next, the grid was flattened into a single long list and passed to two fully connected layers of 1,024 nodes each, followed by a dropout layer with a rate of 0.5. Dropout randomly switches off half of the nodes during training, which stops the network from leaning too heavily on any one of them. After the last dropout came a final layer with as many nodes as there were subfields to predict, using a softmax. The network was trained with stochastic gradient descent, with a learning rate of 0.01, a nesterov momentum of 0.9 and a decay of 0.000001. It learned from batches of 64 articles, and one epoch (the point at which the learning rate was reduced) was counted after 11,000 articles had been processed. The network was trained on a random sample of 24,000,000 articles.

We also tested two simpler machine learning methods, a support vector machine (SVM) and logistic regression. Both work by finding a boundary or a rule that separates the different categories. Both were based on how often each word or short phrase appears in a paper, adjusted for how common it is across all papers. This measure is called term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF). We used it for single words (1-grams) and for pairs of words (2-grams). We kept the 150,000 words and phrases with the highest TF–IDF scores. We trained the SVM and logistic regression models on 1 million articles. We did not need to train them on more, because early tests showed that the models did not improve after 0.75 million articles.

### Bibliographic coupling

For each paper P and each subfield S, we calculated a similarity score based on bibliographic coupling and adjusted it as follows:

BCsimilarityp,s=∑x∈Xlog(x)T

Here, X is the set of all bibliographic coupling values between paper P and all the other papers in subfield S, and T is the total number of citations given by all the papers in subfield S.

### Direct citation

For each paper P and each subfield S, we calculated a similarity score based on direct citation and adjusted it as follows:

DCsimilarityp,s=log(1+inCits)1+log(1+subfieldNR)+log(1+outCits)1+log(1+paperNR)

Here, inCits is the number of times paper P was cited by all the papers in subfield S, and outCits is the number of times paper P cited subfield S. subfieldNR is the total number of citations given by subfield S, and paperNR is the total number of citations given by paper P. In the end, paper P is placed in the subfield S with the highest DCsimilarity score. We calculated this score for every paper against every subfield.

### How we judged the results

Bibliometricians and machine learning researchers judge sorting tasks in different ways. In bibliometrics, the goal is often to find the "true" sorting, but there are no clear gold standard collections of answers for sorting individual scientific papers. A gold standard is a set of answers that everyone agrees is correct. To make up for this lack, and to try to measure sorting systems with numbers, the concentration of a review's references (the Herfindahl index) is currently used as the measure for this task (we say more about this below) [6].

In machine learning research, it has become standard to split the data into three parts: a training set, a validation set and a test set. The model learns from the training set, is checked on the validation set, and is finally tested on the test set. Unfortunately, this was not strictly possible here, because the citation-based methods (direct citation and bibliographic coupling) do not work well with such a split. More importantly, the training set we used is only a rough stand-in for what we want to achieve, not the true answer.

In fact, the training set was made by roughly labelling each article with the label of its journal, which works for journals that cover a single subject. But our task is to sort each article on its own, whatever its journal. Because of this, 56% of the articles in the training set matched the most common label given by 5 experts. Even so, we still present these standard measures in the supplementary material. Instead, we focus on two other ways of judging the results: a gold standard built by hand by people, which we used as our test set, and the Herfindahl index.

We measured performance for both the methods that sort individual papers and the methods that sort journals. We should point out, though, that the bibliometrics community is clearly moving towards sorting individual papers wherever possible, for the reasons given above. Also, the measures for methods that sort journals are only as good as the citation-based methods that were used earlier to build the Science-Metrix system.

#### Comparison with the training set

We calculated five scores: precision, recall, specificity, sensitivity and F1. Precision asks how often a label was right when the model gave it. Recall asks how many of the truly labelled papers the model found. Specificity and sensitivity ask how well the model tells apart the other categories. F1 combines precision and recall into a single number.

To calculate these scores, we used the whole dataset rather than splitting it into training, validation and test parts. We did this because bibliographic coupling and direct citation do not work well with such a split, and splitting would have tilted the results in their favour. Also, in all the machine learning cases, the training data were smaller than the validation data. This limits how much overfitting could have muddled the results. Overfitting happens when a model learns the quirks of its training data too closely and then does worse on new data. On top of that, the training set is not the true answer: only 56% of its articles matched the most common label given by 5 experts. In other words, 44% of the labels in the training set were not assigned as well as they could have been. This makes these scores much less meaningful, so we present their results in the supplementary material.

We compared the methods with the training set mainly to follow the usual practice in machine learning. But readers should treat these results with great caution, because 44% of the labels in the training set were not assigned as well as they could have been. We did not use any statistical tests, because we calculated precision, recall, specificity, sensitivity and F1 on the whole dataset that matters for this task (that is, the whole population), rather than on a few random samples [26].

#### Benchmark 1 (B1): How tightly references are bunched into subjects (Herfindahl index)

Following Klavans and Boyack [6], we calculated a citation concentration score for every article with 100 or more references that could be sorted, meaning the journals they cited were among the journals that had been sorted. This method rests on an assumption. Large review articles tend to give a full account of a topic, summing up a large amount of earlier research from a single or a few research subfields and specialties. In other words, if everything else is equal, review papers would naturally gather together papers on related topics. That makes them good reference points for measuring how tightly papers are bunched into a subject. So a more accurate sorting method should give a higher Herfindahl index. Boyack and Klavans [27, 28] seem to have been the first to use the Herfindahl index as a measure of accuracy for sorting papers into subjects. The Herfindahl index has also been used in a small number of unrelated studies to measure how tightly, and in which direction, large groups of peer-reviewed articles are cited, that is, how widely they are taken up [29].

The Herfindahl index first came from economics, where it measures how much a market is dominated by a few players. Over the last ten years it has been used to measure how tightly citations are bunched within a collection of papers [29]. It has also been used to measure how varied the subjects of citations are. However, Klavans and Boyack's use of the index to measure how well papers are grouped together seems to us to be new.

We calculated Herfindahl index scores for 379,413 papers. We worked out how tightly references were bunched into each subfield, using the Herfindahl index, for DL, for bibliographic coupling and for direct citation, at both the article level and the journal level.

#### Benchmark 2 (B2): Sorting articles by hand

To build a test set, we asked five bibliometric analysts to sort, by hand, the same set of 100 scientific papers picked at random from journals that cover a single subject. We asked six other analysts to do the same for another set of 100 articles from journals that cover many subjects. We asked the analysts to sort the papers as well as they could, using whatever information they had. Most of them used search engines to find out more about the authors and the institutions they work at. When analysts were unsure, they could give a paper more than one subfield, and in that case we asked them to rank the subfields by how relevant each was.

For each of the three computer methods, we calculated the percentage of papers that the computer and the analysts sorted in the same way. As the target, we used the subfield that the analysts most often chose as their first choice. When there was a tie, we kept all the top subfields, and a computer category earned a point if it matched one of them.
parts.results:
## Results

Our first check of how well each sorting method worked was to compare it with Science-Metrix, the sorting system we used to teach the computer methods. Science-Metrix is a ready-made system that sorts journals into subjects, and it served as our training data.

To judge the methods, we used two scores. Precision tells us how often a method's label is right. The F1 score combines precision with recall, which is how many of the truly correct labels the method actually finds. We worked out both scores in two ways. The first is an ordinary average. The second, called the macro-average, gives each subject equal weight, so that subjects with many papers do not drown out subjects with few.

Deep learning tended to copy the Science-Metrix sorting more closely than bibliographic coupling and direct citation did. It had a higher macro-averaged F1 score, and a much higher macro-averaged precision, than the other two methods (S3 Table). S1 Table gives the precision for each subject.

When we sorted journals, however, all three methods did better than any of them did when sorting individual papers (S3 Table). This is easy to explain, because Science-Metrix itself sorts journals.

We also looked at the pairs of subjects that the computer methods most often swapped. For each paper, we checked which subject the method gave it and which subject Science-Metrix gave it, and we counted how often the two differed. In general, the two subjects in these pairs were about the same kind of science.

Here are some examples. Science-Metrix placed a paper in the subject Automobile design & engineering. Deep learning put it in Networking & telecommunications 65% of the time, and direct citation 59% of the time. Economic theory was swapped with Economics 51% of the time (direct citation 34%). Mining & metallurgy was confused with Materials 47% of the time for deep learning (23% for direct citation). Horticulture was swapped with Plant biology & botany 42% of the time for deep learning (39% for direct citation). S2 Table gives the full results.

Taken together, these results show that very different methods can come to a similar sorting of journals. This first set of results should be read with caution. Science-Metrix is not a perfect system: it sorted journals correctly only 53% of the time. We used it as our training data, and we had no better "gold standard", a perfect answer key, to compare against.

Next, we looked at the Herfindahl index, a score of how tightly a paper's references are concentrated in a few subjects. A score of 0 means the references are spread evenly across all subjects, and a score of 1 means they all belong to one subject. We worked out this score for every paper and every journal, for each of the three methods. We then took the median, the middle value when all the scores are lined up from lowest to highest.

The median scores for the three methods (Benchmark 1) were not very different. For individual papers, deep learning scored lowest, at 0.35, compared with 0.39 for bibliographic coupling and 0.43 for direct citation. For journals, deep learning and direct citation tied at 0.29, with bibliographic coupling slightly lower at 0.27 (Fig 3).

Deep learning had the lowest median for papers because it had fewer high scores, not because it had more low scores. You can see this in Fig 3. The violin shapes show how many papers had each score, and the wider a violin is, the more papers there were at that score. The box plots show the middle half of the scores. The bottom parts of the violins are equally wide for all three methods, and so are the lower boxes. The top parts of the violins, though, are narrowest for deep learning.

Fig 3

Herfindahl scores for the three sorting methods, for individual papers and for journals.

The curves show how all 379,413 Herfindahl scores are spread out for each method. The pale grey, thicker vertical lines are outliers, scores far from the rest.

Fig 4 shows how the Herfindahl scores differ between each pair of methods, for both papers and journals. To make each comparison, we took the scores in one row and subtracted the scores in one column. Each comparison used the scores for all 379,413 papers that had more than 100 references in common with other papers.

For individual papers, deep learning's Herfindahl score was 0.04 lower than bibliographic coupling's and 0.07 lower than direct citation's. The results also show that, for every method, sorting individual papers always gave better scores than sorting journals.

The score in each row is subtracted from the score in each column. Each comparison uses the scores for all 379,413 papers with more than 100 references in common. A green cell means the method in the row gave more concentrated scores than the method in the column, and a red cell means the opposite.

Benchmark 2 (B2) compares the computer methods with sorting by hand. Usually, the subjects chosen by the experts were related to each other, but the experts sometimes disagreed a lot. For example, for one paper, two experts chose the subject biophysics, while the others chose anatomy & morphology, bioinformatics, biomedical engineering or evolutionary biology (Table 3). In one case, the five experts placed a paper in five different subjects and in four different fields of science. Another kind of disagreement happened when a paper covered several subjects or had uses in several areas (see the third paper in Table 3).

In contrast, direct citation and bibliographic coupling always gave the same answer for a paper, even when the experts disagreed overall. In many cases, the computer methods' answers stayed believable, even when they differed from what the experts agreed on.

Overall, Benchmark 2 shows that the computer methods were more accurate than sorting by hand. It also shows that the methods' scores were more alike in the disciplinary dataset than in the multidisciplinary dataset (Fig 5). The disciplinary dataset is made of papers from a single field of science, and the multidisciplinary dataset is made of papers that cross several fields.

In both datasets, all the computer methods performed at a broadly similar level. To check this, we used 95% confidence intervals, a range that shows how uncertain each method's average score is. For every pair of methods, these ranges overlapped.

Discussion

We looked at how much each sorting method differed from the others. The differences were small, so we can say that, overall, each method works about as well as the other two. This suggests that it does not make a huge difference whether we sort papers with direct citation, bibliographic coupling or deep learning when we want to fit them into an existing sorting system. Even so, it is clear that measures are always more precise when they are based on sorting each paper on its own, as earlier work has also shown [6].

Our tests did not show deep learning beating the other methods overall. But it also worked just as well as bibliographic coupling and direct citation at sorting papers from journals that cover a single subject and from journals that cover many subjects (test B2). Deep learning did not do as well as the two citation-based methods in the test of how tightly references are concentrated in a subject (test B1), either for single papers or for journals. Still, it did not fall behind them by much.

Direct citation seemed to do slightly better overall. For review papers, which list a large number of references, it gave a high concentration of references in a subject (test B1). It also agreed with experts as much as the other methods did (test B2).

Direct citation and bibliographic coupling are well-established methods. They have been used on a large scale for about ten years, and they have been tried out at many different scales for nearly fifty years. Our paper shows that these methods can be used effectively to move from sorting journals to sorting individual papers, for an existing sorting system of science. This works as long as there is a starting set of examples to learn from. We used the Science-Metrix sorting system to give each paper the subject of the journal it was published in. This is quite different from the bottom-up approach, where similar papers are grouped together first and the groups then form larger categories, which is often done with these measures of how alike papers are.

As several earlier studies have reported, different sorting methods come with trade-offs, and it may be hard to pick out one that is clearly better than the others [17, 20]. The results of our experiment support the view that there is a toolkit of sorting methods available. It can handle the many different sources of information, situations, goals and audiences that bibliometrics deals with.

The methods we used in this experiment made it possible to sort both papers and journals. This lets them keep up with the sorting systems that people already use. For example, the deep learning method for sorting individual papers that we present here was recently used to improve the sorting system behind the production of bibliometric data. This was part of the National Science Board's Science and Engineering Indicators 2020 series of reports. The method made it possible to move papers from journals that cover many subjects into the 176 subjects of the Science-Metrix sorting system. That effort also aimed to make the results match the National Science Foundation's own Taxonomy of Disciplines, its own system for sorting research into subjects.

Using the same sorting system for papers and for journals has given results that further support sorting science by individual papers when calculating measures for single papers. Sorting papers one by one gives more precise results than using the subjects of journals to sort papers, as people often do when they use the National Science Foundation's journal-based sorting system or the ones offered by Web of Science and Scopus.

Deep learning has the benefit of being able to sort papers even when there is no information about their references or citations. More work is needed to confirm this possibility. Deep learning also has the potential to bring together kinds of information that have usually been kept apart. As a first step toward this, our version of the deep learning model combined three kinds of information. The first was information about the topic, taken from the titles, keywords and abstracts. The second was information about where the authors work, such as the names of their departments. The third was citation information, in the form of how the paper's references were spread across subjects. The model learned the right weight to give each of these kinds of information while it was being trained.

It is also possible that the Herfindahl index, a score of how tightly a paper's references are concentrated in a few subjects, could be built into the loss function, the score the network tries to make as small as it learns. That would let the model learn to make that score as good as possible. Finally, nothing stops us from adding information from bibliographic coupling and direct citation to the model. Deep learning therefore looks very promising as a way to help sort both journals and papers, at low cost, when dealing with huge amounts of data.
